name: Tara Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we aren't selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lectures Monday to Thursday for civil engineering, a surveying field trip on Wednesdays when the weather allows, and church choir practice on Thursday evening. Saturdays I work the early shift at Ridley's Bakery, up at five. I live in student housing with five others, and I go home to the farm every second weekend if I can afford the train.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's my dad's, about a hundred and forty acres of dairy and some wheat, three hours away. My grandad worked it before him. Mum works part-time at the village shop and does the farm's paperwork at night. I'm the eldest, and my brother Jonas is sixteen and wants to farm. I want to build the bridges and drains that the countryside needs, and I'd like to go back eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's what I thought. People get excited about every new gadget, and then the milk still has to be collected at six. I wouldn't make a fuss. I'd keep quiet and get on with my work, and maybe tell the choir that some things stay the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, but the farm is still the worry. Milk prices have been low, and Dad has loans on the new parlour. My degree is a way to bring some steadier money into the family. If AI doesn't change much, then I just have to get through the course and find a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. Study hard, keep the bakery shifts, and apply for a summer placement with the county roads department. I'd send some of my wage home when I can, even if Dad says no. And I'd keep not using the AI helpers, because I'd rather learn the work properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. A bit uneasy about the farm's money, but that's a worry I've lived with since I was little. It isn't new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the farm's loan keeps you awake. What would happen if milk prices dropped again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use AI because I want to understand the ground I'm building on. In a bridge you can't guess, and if you can't explain a calculation then you shouldn't sign it. I'd rather get a worse mark and know the answer than copy something I can't check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's behind your choice not to use AI helpers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm's loan is the thing that keeps me awake. If milk prices drop again, Dad would sell some heifers, and that's a bad sign. Mum says we've been through bad years before, and we always got through them together. That's what I hold on to.

say: I'd say **I thought so**: people get excited and the milk still gets collected at six.
I'd keep quiet and tell the choir that some things **stay the same**.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, but the **farm's loan** is still the worry.
My degree can bring **steadier money** into the family.
do: Study hard and keep the **bakery shifts**.
Apply for a summer placement with the **county roads department**.
Send some wages **home** even if Dad says no.
feel: **Steady**, with a long-held worry about the farm's money.
S0.quote: If you can't explain a calculation then you shouldn't sign it.
fieldNote: Tara's worry is the **farm's loan**, not AI, and she holds it quietly.
Her no-AI view comes from **professional duty**: a bridge calculation must be understood.
Her family tone is firm and loyal, and sending wages home shows it.

steps.text: Keep the early Saturday shift at Ridley's Bakery
Apply for a summer placement with the roads department
Send part of my bakery wage home each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, it'll change some office jobs, and that's fine, but we shouldn't forget the people who work with their hands. I'd say it at church and at home. I'd say we need good apprenticeships and not just courses on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the checking and drawing side of my degree is the risky part. Engineers do a lot of calculations and drawings, and a program could take that over. The part that stays is being on site with mud on your boots, and I'm happy to do that. So I think I'd be okay, but fewer people would get in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd push for site-based work. I'd ask the roads department about an apprenticeship-style placement. And I'd have to face using the software once I'm in a job, because refusing would just get me fired. I'd do it slowly and check it twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. It's not the end of the world. It's the sense that the path I chose might get narrower, and Dad would say, what did we pay for?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Dad would ask what the family paid for. What would you say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At home, the changes would show up in the paperwork first. Mum already spends hours on milk records and subsidy forms. If a program did them, she'd have her evenings back, and I'd like that. The farm itself would carry on the same, since cows still have to be milked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jonas to learn a skill with his hands and a skill with numbers. A farmer now needs both. He wants to farm, and I'd tell him that's honest work, but that he should also know what a tractor's computer is doing.

say: I'd say it will change **office jobs**, but don't forget people who work with their hands.
I'd ask for **apprenticeships**, not just screen courses.
think: The **checking and drawing** side of my degree is the risky part.
**Site work** will stay, and I'm happy with mud on my boots.
do: Push for **site-based work** and ask about an apprenticeship-style placement.
Learn the software slowly once in a job and **check it twice**.
Tell my brother to learn **hands and numbers**.
feel: **Uneasy**, worried the path I chose might get narrower.
S1.quote: The part that stays is being on site with mud on your boots, and I'm happy to do that.
fieldNote: Tara trusts **site work** as her protected ground, which suits her rural and traditional view.
She accepts the software as a **job requirement** but will do it slowly and carefully.
Her advice to her brother Jonas shows her care for the farm's next generation.

steps.text: Ask the roads department for a site-based placement
Learn the design software only when a job needs it
Tell Jonas to learn tractor computers and farm accounts
Keep going with the civil engineering course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not right that something like that can come with only two years' warning. Families and farms can't change that fast. I'd say it at church, and I'd say the people who build these systems have a duty to people who work for a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be very worried. If the thinking work goes in two years, I'd be at the end of my second year. My degree and our loan for my fees could be wasted. And Dad's farm needs money from somewhere, and I can't see where, if jobs vanish and people buy less milk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk with Dad about the farm before anything else. I'd pull back on spending and take extra shifts at the bakery. I'd stay on the course, because walking away would feel like giving up, but I'd look at hands-on trades, like site surveying, that might last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd pray about it, and I'm not ashamed to say that. It would help me get through the days without getting stuck in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the farm might outlast the office. How does that change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the thinking part goes first, then the hands-on part has three years. Cows and fields might be last, since a robot that milks and mucks out is hard to build. That gives me a kind of hope. The farm might outlast the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the effect reach your family from the side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What scares me is the stuff in between, like shops, banks and the milk buyer's offices. If those places cut staff, then people have less money, and fewer people can buy milk. That's how it gets to us, from the side.

say: I'd say **two years** is not fair warning, because families and farms can't change that fast.
I'd say builders of these systems have a **duty** to working people.
think: My **degree** and the loan for my fees could be wasted.
The farm needs money from somewhere if **jobs vanish** and people buy less milk.
do: Talk with **Dad** about the farm's money first.
Take **extra bakery shifts** and cut spending.
Look at **hands-on trades** like site surveying.
feel: **Anxious**, and I'd pray about it to get through the days.
S2.quote: Cows and fields might be last, since a robot that milks and mucks out is hard to build.
fieldNote: Tara finds a **hopeful thread**: hands-on farm work may last longer than office work.
Her fear is **indirect**: shops, banks and buyers cut staff and demand for milk falls.
She mentions prayer openly as a way of coping, which shows her faith's role.

steps.text: Sit down with Dad and review the farm's loan
Take extra Saturday and Sunday bakery shifts
Look into site surveying courses and apprenticeships
Ask the church community about help for the farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people are sensible. I'd tell my friends to learn something practical and not to rely on one skill. I'd say it to the choir, too. We can look after one another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be on the edge. I'd finish my degree in 2029 and start work in a year when everything's about to change. I'd have two years of pay before the thinking work goes, and I'd use them to get Dad's loan down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate and go to work for a firm that builds on site, like drainage and roads. I'd send money home every month. And I'd talk to Mum about whether the farm should take on any new debt, because I wouldn't advise it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. Five years feels like enough time for something to be done, and not enough to relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the farm not relying on milk alone. What else could it do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas would be 21 by then, and finishing at agricultural college. I'd want him to have a proper plan for the farm. If both of us can bring in money, the farm doesn't have to rely on milk alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell your mum you'd help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would be the one to hold everyone together, as always. I'd want her to hear it from me that I'll help. She won't ask, so I'd have to say it first.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** to get ready if people are sensible.
I'd tell friends to learn something **practical** and not rely on one skill.
think: I'd be **on the edge**, starting work right before everything changes.
My first **two years of pay** could pay down Dad's loan.
do: Work for a firm that builds **on site**, like drainage and roads.
Advise Mum **against new debt** on the farm.
feel: **Anxious** but steady: enough time for something to be done, not to relax.
S3.quote: If both of us can bring in money, the farm doesn't have to rely on milk alone.
fieldNote: Tara plans around her **family's farm**, using her first working years to help with its loan.
She includes her brother Jonas in the plan, picturing a farm with **two incomes**.
She worries about telling her mum directly, because her mum won't ask for help.

steps.text: Apply to drainage and road-building firms for a graduate job
Send a fixed amount home each month
Plan the farm's future with Mum and Jonas
Keep my own spending low through the first job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and a good chance. I'd tell people to learn a trade and to look after their families. It's nothing to be afraid of if you get ready, and I'd say it at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel steady. Ten years gets me through my degree, a few years working, and maybe I'd be back near the farm. The thing I'd worry about is Dad getting older. In ten years he'd be sixty-two, and the farm would need a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a few years on site, and save for a house near home. I'd learn the software as I go, because I'd have to. And I'd keep close to the church and the choir, because they keep me steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, not at the front. It's the kind of thing you plan for, like the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the low field floods each winter. What would you do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to bring skills back to the farm. A surveyor knows about drainage and land levels, and our low field floods every winter. That's the kind of thing a civil engineer could fix, and it would save Dad money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be steady in your own life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, I'd also want to marry and have a family in that time. Whatever happens with the jobs, I'd want something steady in my own life. That's what I've seen at home.

say: I'd say ten years is **a good chance** and nothing to fear if you get ready.
I'd tell people to **learn a trade** and look after their families.
think: I'd feel **steady**, but Dad would be sixty-two and the farm needs a **plan**.
My worry is **at the back** of my mind, not the front.
do: Finish the degree and work **on site** for a few years.
Stay close to the **church and choir**.
feel: **Uneasy** at the back of my mind, like the weather.
S4.quote: Our low field floods every winter. That's the kind of thing a civil engineer could fix, and it would save Dad money.
fieldNote: Tara pictures her **degree serving the farm**, such as fixing the flooding low field.
She wants a steady family life, a very **traditional** goal she says plainly.
Faith and community are her anchors across all five scenarios.

steps.text: Finish the civil engineering degree on schedule
Save for a house near the family farm
Plan the low field drainage with Dad
Move back to the home region after two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. Two years isn't enough for a farm to change anything, or for me to finish what I started. What would help is clear honesty from the people in charge, loans that don't crush a family, and apprenticeships that give young people a real way in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me get told we're stuck in the past because we don't use the new tools. I'm not stuck. I just think work should be understood by the person doing it, and I'd say that about a bridge or a cow.

headlineQuote: I just think work should be understood by the person doing it, and I'd say that about a bridge or a cow.
portrait: Tara is an **18-year-old** civil engineering student from a dairy farm who works early Saturdays at a bakery.
She sings in a church choir and her faith and **family loyalty** shape her choices.
She is traditional and resistant, and does not use AI because a **calculation must be understood** before signing it.
Her fear is **indirect**: shops, banks and buyers cut staff, so fewer people buy milk.
She aims to bring her skills **back to the farm**, such as fixing the flooding low field.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario worries her most, because a farm cannot change in that time.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest leaders**, family-friendly loans and apprenticeships that give young people a real way in.
